summary:
Johor is one of Malaysia's thirteen states and stands under the national framework, which criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity at two levels. Sections 377A to 377D of the federal Penal Code punish same-sex intimacy and "outrages on decency" with up to twenty years' imprisonment plus whipping, apply to men and women alike, reach non-citizens, and extend to conduct that would be lawful and private elsewhere. Every state and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya also maintain Sharia enactments prohibiting cross-dressing and "males posing as females", with penalties of up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning; those state offences reach Muslims only.

Johor's own record contains no protective or tolerant regime. In November 2023 the Johor government announced plans to establish conversion-therapy centres to "rehabilitate" LGBT people, and public-morality offences in the state are enforced through its religious authorities rather than through any licensing or consent framework.

The hostile climate in Johor sits inside a national pattern. A crackdown on LGBT people has run since the 2018 general election; at least 1,733 people had attended state "rehabilitation programmes" by June 2021, and state-conducted investigations have covered Kuala Lumpur, Selangor, Negeri Sembilan, Kelantan, Penang, Pahang and Kedah, showing that enforcement is directed from state apparatus across the country rather than confined to any single unit.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the Sharia cross-dressing offences do not apply, but the Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest and public outing at specific venues, where detainees' identities have been leaked to media and foreign nationals have required embassy intervention.
tangentialFactors:
Johor's conversion-therapy announcement is not an outlier measure but a state-level expression of a national posture: government-funded mukhayyam "rehabilitation" retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, LGBT events and media content are censored, and Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform prospects.

The federal layer has proved more durable than the state Sharia layer. The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and sixteen Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds, yet Penal Code offences remained fully intact, so litigation that narrows Sharia reach does not narrow a visitor's exposure under sections 377A to 377D.

There is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law anywhere in Malaysia, and no legal definition in any state enactment of what constitutes transgender dressing, leaving the scope of "males posing as females" to the discretion of enforcing officers.
localsOnly:
Sharia cross-dressing and same-sex offences reach Muslims only. Non-Muslim residents fall outside the state religious enactments but remain subject to the federal Penal Code, so the distinction shields no one from sections 377A to 377D.

Public-morality and gender-nonconformity offences in Johor are enforced by state religious authorities, which operate without a statutory definition of transgender presentation. Since the 1980s all thirteen states have passed such enactments, and three of them also bar women from posing as men.

Residents are the target population for the conversion-therapy centres announced by the Johor government in November 2023 and for the national rehabilitation programmes that had enrolled at least 1,733 people by June 2021.

Documented enforcement elsewhere in the country indicates what residents can expect in Johor: arrests of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014 that prompted a constitutional challenge, the mobilisation of 122 religious officers against Nur Sajat before she fled to Thailand and obtained UNHCR protection, and a public order in July 2020 from the Religious Affairs Minister giving the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department his "full licence to carry out its enforcement actions" against transgender persons.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory confirms whether the conversion-therapy centres announced by the Johor government in November 2023 have been built, opened or funded; the announcement is on record, the operational status is unresolved.

Johor-specific arrest, charge and caning figures are not sourced here. The seven states named in the 2022 investigation coverage do not include Johor, and the inventory does not state whether Johor conducted comparable investigations or whether it did so without recording them.

Whether whipping under sections 377A to 377D has been carried out against a foreign visitor in Johor is not documented in these sources; the assessment that tourists are rarely targeted rests on the reported pattern of enforcement rather than on Johor-specific visitor case data.

Source currency is uneven: the Human Dignity Trust profile was updated on 16 December 2025, while the joint Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters reporting dates from 10 August 2022 and the rehabilitation attendance figure to June 2021.
